title: Lube a bike chain: drip lube onto the chain while the other hand turns the pedal backwards
instruction: Lube the bike chain: drip the lube onto the chain while turning the crank backwards.
context: Lubing the chain is the commonest piece of home bicycle upkeep: a dry chain squeaks, wears and rusts. It is done with the bike held still, one hand turning a pedal backwards so the chain runs past, the other holding a drip bottle over the chain and squeezing so each link gets a drop. Lube that misses lands on the tyre, the rim or the floor, and a flooded chain collects grit, so the bottle is carried without squeezing, squeezed only over the chain, and stood back upright afterwards. The task tests two hands doing different things at once on one object: one keeps a narrow target moving at a steady pace, the other holds a squeeze bottle on that moving target, 9 mm wide, and doses it.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table: x forward (away from the robot), y to the robot's left; heights above the table. (1) A whole 14 inch child's pedal bike with a freewheel rear hub and no chain guard (the light kind with hand brakes; a back-pedal brake or a full chain guard rules a bike out), about 103 cm long and 6 to 7 kg, standing upright across the table in two wheel stands screwed to the table (each a 13 by 16 cm foot with two cheeks 7 cm high gripping the tyre). The bike's middle plane is at x 42, its chain side toward the robot, rear wheel toward the robot's left, front wheel toward its right: rear axle at y 31, front axle at y -36, both 17.8 cm up (wheels 35.6 cm across with 4 cm tyres). The cranks' axle is at x 42, y 9, 21 cm up. Single-speed drive: 26-tooth chainring and 14-tooth freewheel cog, their axles 22.7 cm apart, a 1/2 by 1/8 inch chain of 56 links running 4.2 cm to the robot's side of the bike's middle plane (x 37.8), with about 1 cm of slack in its lower run. Cranks 8 cm long; flat pedals 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 1.8 cm thick that turn freely on their spindles. At the start the near (chain-side) crank hangs down, its pedal centred at x 31, y 8, 13 cm up. Handlebars 42 cm wide at y -26, 55 cm up; saddle at y 20, 47 cm up. The chain is clean and dry. (2) A 118 ml (4 oz) soft plastic squeeze bottle of chain lube with a drip nozzle, cap removed, 3.8 cm across and 12 cm tall, about 130 g, standing upright on the table at x 24, y 40, in front of the rear wheel. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial from two things: which of the chain's 56 links have lube on them, and how the place is left. Drops: a drop leaves the bottle each 0.45 s that its nozzle points at least 20 degrees below level and its wall is squeezed in at least 3 mm on each side (24 N a side in the simulator; a carrying grip of up to 18 N stays dry). A drop falls straight down. It wets a link if it lands within 6 mm of the middle line of the chain, on the first link below the nozzle; otherwise it is a miss. A link is wet once one drop has landed on it. Score: 0 with fewer than 14 wet links (this includes doing nothing, and squeezing over a chain that is not moving, which wets one or two links); 0.25 with 14 to 27 wet links; 0.5 with 28 to 49; 0.75 with 50 or more; 1.0 with 50 or more wet links and the place left tidy, all at the same moment: the bottle standing on the table (its base within 1 cm of the table top, within 10 degrees of upright, moving less than 1 cm/s), each gripper's fingertip centre more than 11 cm from the middle of the bottle and more than 5 cm from the near pedal's centre, and the cranks turning slower than 0.1 rad/s. The score is capped at 0.5 (0.25 with fewer than 28 wet links) if more than 12 drops missed the chain, if more than 140 drops were released in all (two and a half a link: guides say one drop a roller), or if any of the chain has been pushed more than 5 mm off its line, off the teeth. Which way the cranks turn, how the bottle is held and where along the chain the drops land are not scored. Real trial: use lube tinted with a UV or oil-soluble dye; mark one outer link with a paint pen as link 1; lay a white sheet under the drivetrain and tape white paper over the rear tyre and rim beside the chain. Afterwards turn the cranks by hand under a lamp and count the links showing dye on their rollers or plates (wet links); count the spots on the sheet, paper, frame and stays (misses); weigh the bottle before and after to 0.01 g and divide by the weight of one drop from that bottle (about 0.04 g, measured beforehand over 20 drops) for the drops released; a photo shows the bottle upright and the grippers clear; the chain is on its teeth if it runs when the crank is turned.
reset_notes: About 15 minutes a trial. Wipe the chain with degreaser on a rag while back-pedalling until a clean rag comes away clean, then dry it; wipe any lube off the frame, tyre and rim; replace the white sheet and paper. Top the bottle up to its start weight (within 1 g), wipe its nozzle, and stand it back on its mark (within 5 mm). Turn the cranks so the near pedal hangs down. Check the wheel stands are tight. Protect the gripper pads with fresh covers: chain lube must not reach them. In simulation, run with -E object_jitter=0 -E device=cpu; every reset puts the chain, cranks and bottle back and dries every link.
fidelity: Chain: 56 separate rigid links on pin joints, driven only by the teeth (ratio measured 1.86, 26/14 = 1.857); rollers are spheres fixed to their links, link inertia 6x real. Frame, wheels and stands are fixed plain shapes; the rear wheel is fixed. Bottle: rigid core with four sprung wall pads, stiffer than real (drips at 24 N a side). No liquid: drops are counted by rule, fall straight and wet one link; no running or wicking. CPU physics. The demo reads nozzle and crank positions each second.
scores: Demo (scripted): 1.0, reached at step 1,726 of 3,000. Dream-1 (dreamlabs/dream-1-beta): 0, ran to the 3,000-step limit.
